explanation: Classic inferior STEMI: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. Inferior wall is RCA-supplied in ~80% (right-dominant). STE greater in III than II favors RCA over LCx; check V4R for RV involvement.
Anterior STEMI: ST elevation across V1-V4 from LAD occlusion. Large territory at risk and high mortality. Reciprocal inferior depression may appear.
Anteroseptal STEMI: ST elevation focused in V1-V3 from proximal LAD occlusion involving septal perforators. Loss of septal r-wave may be seen.
Anterolateral STEMI: extensive ST elevation across the precordium plus I and aVL from a proximal LAD (often wrapping) occlusion. Large territory; watch for pump failure.
Lateral STEMI: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5, V6 from LCx occlusion, with reciprocal inferior depression. High-lateral (I/aVL) changes can be subtle.

Posterior STEMI: horizontal ST DEPRESSION with tall R waves in V1-V3 is the mirror image of posterior injury. Confirm with posterior leads V7-V9 showing elevation. Often accompanies inferior/lateral MI.
RV STEMI: inferior STE with STE III > II and elevation in V1; confirm with V4R. Preload-dependent - avoid nitrates. Proximal RCA occlusion before the RV marginal branch.
Normal ECG. No pathologic ST elevation; J-points at baseline, T waves concordant and proportionate. No reciprocal changes.
Benign early repolarization mimic: concave ST elevation with notched J-points, most prominent in mid-precordial leads, no reciprocal depression, stable over time.
Pericarditis mimic: diffuse concave ST elevation across multiple territories with PR-segment depression (and PR elevation in aVR), without a coronary distribution or reciprocal change.
